incidents.cause: The pilots failure to maintain clearance from terrain resulting in an in-flight collision with a house. Contributing to the accident was the night instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and the pilot's lack of experience of flying in IMC.
The pilot's failure to control the helicopter while maneuvering, resulting in loss of tail rotor effectiveness.
The pilot’s failure to see and avoid power lines while maneuvering near the ground because dust stirred up by the rotor wash obscured his visibility.
An in-flight loss of control for undetermined reasons.
The pilot's improper preflight performance planning, which resulted in a hard landing due to low rotor rpm while operating near maximum gross weight in high density altitude conditions.
A total loss of tail rotor effectiveness.   Contributing to the accident was the pilot's improper decision to operate inside the height velocity curve.
The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from the power transmission lines.  Contributing to the accident was the unmarked power transmission lines.
The in-flight separation of the tail rotor gear box for an undetermined reason. Contributing to the accident was the hilly terrain, which was unsuitable for a forced landing.

The student's inadvertent control interference, which the flight instructor was unable to overcome. A contributing factor was the instructor's poor crew coordination in his failure to verbally command the student to relinquish the controls and his inadequate supervision of the flight.
The pilot's improper recovery from a practice autorotation.

The pilot's failure to ensure that the helicopter was properly loaded, which resulted in the helicopter being in excess of its maximum allowable gross weight and led to a loss of main rotor rpm on takeoff. The pilot's failure to maintain directional control.
The partial loss of engine power during the initial climb and the pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the forced landing with a tailwind.
The pilot under instruction’s improper recovery from a bounced landing and the flight instructor’s delayed remedial action, which resulted in a ground loop and collision with trees.

The pilot of the departing airplane’s failure to see and avoid the landing airplane before takeoff, resulting in a collision with the landing airplane. Contributing was the airport’s failure to encourage pilots to use radios for traffic deconfliction when equipped.

A loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.
The pilot’s loss of directional control during landing with wind gusts, which resulted in a ground loop and collision with a fence.
The pilot's inadequate compensation for the crosswind and failure to maintain directional control.
The pilot's failure to maintain airplane control during landing.
A partial loss of engine power during takeoff due to failure of the left magneto. Contributing to the accident was unsuitable terrain to conduct a forced landing.
The pilot’s loss of control during landing.
An in-flight fire in the engine compartment for undetermined reasons.
The partial loss of engine power due to fuel contamination and partially blocked fuel screens.

The pilot’s descent below surrounding terrain and his delayed decision to initiate a climb which resulted in impact with terrain. Contributing to the accident were terrain and lighting conditions that affected the pilot’s ability to accurately assess terrain clearance.
The pilot's improper decision to continue an aerial application following an uncommanded opening of the cabin door in flight, and his subsequent failure to maintain control of the airplane.
The pilot’s failure to maintain a stabilized approach prior to the retardant drop and his subsequent failure to release the retardant load, resulting in a stall/mush and collision with terrain.

The failure of the starter generator which resulted in the subsequent loss of engine power.  Contributing to the accident were the low altitude at which the airplane was operating, the tall grass, and the ditch.

A total loss of engine power due to the fracture of a single 1st stage compressor rotor airfoil in high-cycle fatigue as a result of the erosion and thinning of the airfoil's leading edge.
